slides.title: A sender in a costume
slides.text: Pim sorts a message that claims to be from the school office. The name on it looks right, but a claimed sender is a costume. That faking is called spoofing, and the real address tells the truth.
slides.alt: A letter named Your Teacher, sent from a stranger's mail box, asks where you live and for your mailbox key.

focus.cue: The real address tells the truth

slides.title: Where does the link go?
slides.text: The words on a link can say one name while the address behind them goes somewhere else. Check the address, not the words.
steps: Address behind them: a stranger's place
Do not tap; verify another way
slides.alt: The faked Post Office letter with every clue found: the real address, the key ask, the rush, and a button that goes elsewhere.

focus.cue: The real address goes somewhere else

slides.title: Aimed at one person
slides.text: Spear phishing uses the same trick recipe, but built for one person. It may use your name, your club or a recent post, then add a rush and a request.
slides.alt: A Fan Club post knows you love skateboards, your dog's name and your birthday, and asks for your key.

focus.cue: Built for one person, from their own posts

slides.title: The attachment rule
slides.text: An unexpected file is not opened, even if the message begs you to hurry. Verify first through a different door: ask the real sender in person, or tell a trusted adult.
slides.alt: A parcel trick: a delivery you never ordered is waiting, and a small fee must be paid within two hours.

focus.cue: An unexpected package, with a pay-now button
Asks for money, two hours to act

slides.title: Reporting protects everyone
slides.text: Reporting a phishing message is a Defender act. One report can warn the whole school and stop the same costume reaching your friends.
slides.alt: The faked Post Office letter, reported: the name says Post Office, but the address and the button tell the truth.

focus.cue: Report it, and the faked sender is blocked

slides.title: Your mission
slides.text: Open Trick Inbox at Faked Senders and sort all 6 messages. For every message, check the real sender before you judge it.
slides.alt: Trick Inbox, Faked Senders: a letter from Post Office says your key expired. Its real address is a freemail box.

focus.cue: Play Faked Senders: check the real address first
